title: Satta and Balvand
hookLine: two minstrels who, tradition says, quarreled with Guru Arjan and were forgiven; their Var is in the Granth (Ramkali, ang 966–968)

lines: TWO MUSICIANS IN THE GURU'S COURT.
cards: Two musicians, a rebab and a voice, singing kirtan in the Guru's court: Satta and Balvand. Then, tradition says, something goes wrong. A request for money, a quarrel, wounded pride.
They stop singing, say hard things about the house they served, and walk out. A falling-out could end right there.
This one ends with their song inside the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Ramkali, Ang 966, kept and sung beside the Gurus' own words.

teach.h: A REQUEST, A QUARREL, A WALKOUT.
teach.b: First the story, as tradition tells it. Satta and Balvand ask Guru Arjan for help, and when it isn't what they hoped, pride takes over. They refuse to play, and boast that the Gurus' fame rests on their music.
Without the court, their fortunes sink.

teach.h: HUMBLED, THEY COME BACK; THE GURU FORGIVES.
teach.b: In the end they come back humbled, asking forgiveness, and tradition says a devoted Sikh pleaded for them. The Guru forgives them, and they pick up the rebab again.
Now the text, which is what the Granth actually keeps: their Var, a ballad, in Raag Ramkali. It doesn't sing about themselves.
It sings about Guru Nanak setting up Lehna as the next Guru, Guru Angad, and the line passing on.

teach.h: THE SAME LIGHT, ONLY THE BODY CHANGED.
teach.b: One of its lines, in paraphrase: the light is the same, the way is the same; the master has only changed the body. It's the claim the Bhatts made yesterday, but listen to who's making it now.
Two men who once claimed the Gurus needed them end up singing that the Guru is one light, needing nothing from anyone, passing from body to body. The quarrel was about who mattered.
The song answers it: the light matters, and everyone else is a singer. And notice what the Guru did.
He didn't just let them back in the door.
Their words went into the scripture, sung in gurdwaras alongside his own. Forgiveness here isn't a grudging truce. It's a microphone handed back.

how: The Var of Satta and Balvand in Raag Ramkali is sung in kirtan like other Gurbani, and Sikhs tell their story as one of pride, return and forgiveness.

o: a quarrel between musicians and a Guru
a ballad, a long poem sung in verses

games.q: inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Var of Satta and Balvand is about their quarrel
it sings of Guru Nanak setting up Guru Angad and the one light passing on.
tradition says the Guru forgave them
they came back humbled, and their Var is in the Granth.
the Var says the light changed when the Guru changed
the light is the same, the way is the same; only the body changed.

games.q: you're the Guru. two singers who walked out and spoke against your house come back, asking forgiveness. what do you do?
o: forgive them, but never let them sing again.
forgive them, and keep their song in the scripture.
games.why: tradition says Guru Arjan forgave them, and their Var is in the Granth, sung alongside the Gurus' own words.

practice: Choose a small quarrel, sized for two minutes: a sharp exchange, a slight, a door that closed, and let the other person's face come to mind.

You don't have to call them or pretend it didn't happen; just loosen your grip on it, one breath at a time, and if something in you is ready, imagine handing them their voice back. If you pray, Waheguru can go with each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Var. A ballad: Satta and Balvand's, in Raag Ramkali, singing that the light is the same, the way is the same, only the body has changed.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a ballad; the Var of Satta and Balvand is set in Raag Ramkali.

carryVoice: Your line: forgiven, and sung. The walkout wasn't the end of their story. See you tomorrow.
